doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Hearing records versus live music, and recording mistakes
summary: Live music is best; on records only the leader's mistakes stop a take while a sideman must catch up.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I wanted to just share with you something that I think is important and then you give me your feedback on it. You know when I listen to music, particularly jazz music and a lot of the great, particular African-American performers, there’s an authenticity in that music that I get that refreshes me, that revitalizes me, it’s something that for instance if I pick up an album of a player that I like and I put that album on, even if I’ve never met that player, I feel like I’ve had a conversation with him you know?

Yeah, because he’s having one with you you know? But the best way to hear music is live if possible. I know it’s impossible for a lot of young people because they can’t afford to go hear music. It’s very expensive to go hear music nowadays. When I come up it was inexpensive to go out and hear music, but we still had to wait until a certain age. So recordings was a way that we had to listen to these guys, you know. And the only thing about recordings is when you make a record, I made a lot of records, you stop, if there’s a mistake made you stop, and you start, if somebody makes a mistake — not the sideman,
only the band leader — if the band leader makes a mistake you stop but if the sideman makes a mistake you better catch up on the next beat.
